A FEW USEFUL COORDINATES

The science behind the view.

This explorer uses NASA's Near Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs). Each row is a predicted Earth close-approach event, not an asteroid's current location.

Positions and the selected path

The default 3D view uses NASA/JPL Horizons geometric state vectors, centered on Earth (399), in the J2000 ecliptic frame. All displayed objects use the same visible UTC epoch. The coordinates are rotated together into the true equatorial frame of the selected date, with Earth’s north up and a nearly equator-level default camera. The raw coordinate readout remains J2000 ecliptic. Positions are linearly scaled together; Earth and point sizes are enlarged. Earth uses georeferenced NASA surface, cloud and night-light composites. Its orientation includes sidereal rotation, axial tilt, precession and nutation at the same UTC epoch as the asteroid positions. Sunlight and the day/night boundary are computed for that date. This is an educational approximation without measured Earth-orientation corrections, not a ground-location or telescope-pointing tool.

Hourly positions and velocities are interpolated with cubic Hermite interpolation. Selecting an object displays only its next 30 days of Earth-relative trajectory, sampled from JPL vectors. It is a predicted flyby track, not a closed orbit around Earth and not an impact forecast. The line is a finite sampled prediction, with no uncertainty envelope. Framing and Earth’s enlarged radius stay fixed while scrubbing. The viewing sphere fixes the distance scale. Changing the radius explicitly changes that scale; selecting an asteroid does not. The path is clipped to the sphere, including separate entry and exit segments. The time slider changes the position epoch; Now sets it to the current time. Live clock follows the current UTC time when it lies within the loaded window. Changing the time input or slider pauses it. Now resumes live time; historical and future windows stay fixed until you change their epoch. Circular grid lines are distance guides, not asteroid orbits.

Directions are no longer arbitrary in 3D. If an object's vectors cannot be retrieved, its dot is omitted and its catalog profile states that its position is unavailable. The separate 2D schematic keeps its original illustrative bearings and log closest-approach distances. Ephemeris dates supported here are 1962–2099. The 3D renderer supports rotation, zoom, keyboard arrows, +/− and Home.

Size, speed and classification

Marker sizes use the midpoint of NASA’s estimated diameter range on a fixed square-root scale, clamped to 5–30 screen pixels. This compresses size differences so small asteroids remain visible. Hollow markers mean diameter unknown. Selecting an asteroid adds a ring without enlarging its size marker. The same scale applies in both views and does not change with filters. Marker sizes are enlarged and are not to the position-distance scale.

Diameters are estimated ranges, not exact measurements. Speeds are relative to Earth at close approach. A lunar distance (LD) is approximately 384,400 km, not the Moon's exact current distance. PHA is NASA's potentially hazardous asteroid classification; it is not an impact probability or warning. See NASA's definition and Sentry impact monitoring for context.

Photos and radar imagery

Confirmed images are matched to NASA object IDs in a reviewed catalog, with their original credits, observation dates and source links. Radar images and processed composites are labeled separately from optical photography. Other profiles query NASA’s Image and Video Library on selection; search matches are explicitly unverified archive candidates, not confirmed photographs of the object. A missing result means no confirmed image is available in these checked sources, not that no image exists anywhere. Images are historical, not live cameras.

Freshness and coverage

Waiting for the data source.

The 30-day timeline uses seven serial NASA requests to collect 44 calendar days: the visible month plus seven days on either side. Only close approaches in the visible timeline appear in the table, metrics and CSV. The 3D field also considers buffered candidates; each dot appears only while its interpolated Earth-center distance lies inside the chosen viewing radius. Every known candidate matching the filters is queued for JPL positions, with progress and failures shown. Objects without coordinates stay omitted. There is no 60-marker cap in 3D. Candidate coverage is limited to this NASA encounter catalog and does not claim to include every asteroid within the sphere. JPL requests load serially, are cached for an hour, and back off on errors. A private NASA key is used when configured; the public demo key is a fallback with lower limits. If NASA is unavailable, a dated saved snapshot uses its actual available timeline and candidate coverage. Refresh incorporates newly reported objects after successful source retrieval; catalog caches refresh after 15 minutes with the personal key (one hour with the demo key). While Live clock is enabled and the page is visible, the app checks for a refresh each minute after the interval expires, preserving the selected asteroid and timeline position. JPL vectors remain cached for one hour.

Snapshots are predictions as retrieved and can be revised. Window metrics summarize the full loaded window; map, table and CSV follow the filters. Daily bars follow search, distance, size and PHA filters before the day selection. The 3D Earth uses historical NASA composites, not live weather or current city-light observations. Blue Marble surface/clouds: NASA/GSFC, Reto Stöckli. Night lights: NASA Earth Observatory/Robert Simmon; Suomi NPP VIIRS data courtesy Chris Elvidge (NOAA NGDC).
